patient_information: A 38-year-old European expatriate male living in Malawi.
chief_complaint: Progressive constipation and difficulty passing urine for the past 3 weeks.
history_of_present_illness: He noticed increasing abdominal pressure to pass urine, eventually only passing small amounts, associated with increasing lower abdominal discomfort, abnormal sensations in the groins and around the genitals, and some erectile dysfunction. He reported no weakness, dysaesthesia, or loss of sensation in his legs, but walking did not feel normal, with no backache. Over 2 months, he experienced unintentional weight loss of 8 kg and fatigue without fever or night sweats, which he blamed on work stress. He has sexual contact only with his wife. One week prior, he noticed reddish discoloration of his urine without painful micturition or fever, was prescribed four medications which he completed. There is no history of trauma and his previous medical history is unremarkable.
exposure_and_epidemiology: He had swum regularly in Lake Malawi.
physical_exam: General examination showed no abnormalities except for a palpable bladder. Rectal examination revealed low anal sphincter tone. Genital examination was normal. Neurological examination showed lively, symmetrical tendon reflexes in the legs without clonus or pathological plantar reflexes, and no other abnormalities.
labs_and_diagnostics: Urine microscopy identified Schistosoma haematobium eggs. An abdominal ultrasound scan showed a large bladder residue without further abnormalities. Full blood count showed a normal absolute WBC of 9 x 10^9/L with relative eosinophilia of 21.8% and an absolute eosinophil count of 1.15 x 10^9/L. ALT was slightly elevated, while creatinine and CRP were normal. HIV and VDRL tests were negative, and stool and urine microscopy were normal. Serological tests for schistosomiasis were not available. An MRI scan of the spinal cord showed an enhancing 1 cm lesion at the anterior aspect of the conus, with associated high T2 signal (oedema) extending to T9, and nodular thickening of the urine bladder wall.
differential_diagnosis: Spinal cord schistosomiasis, spinal tuberculosis, spinal abscess, neurosyphilis, and a tumour or metastases impinging on the conus medullaris.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient required urinary catheterization for 2 weeks. He made a full recovery after a second course of praziquantel and a course of high-dose prednisolone, tapered off over 2 months, and was well after more than 2 years of follow-up.
final_diagnosis: Infection with Schistosoma haematobium, complicated by spinal cord schistosomiasis, as evidenced by urine findings, eosinophilia, and bladder wall abnormalities on MRI.
